title: Horizontal and Vertical Lines
short: y = k is flat with slope 0; x = h is vertical with no slope.
trouble: Students graph x = 3 as a horizontal line, and say a vertical line has slope 0.

blocks.html: Two kinds of lines look too simple to need a lesson, yet they trip people up: flat ones and straight-up ones. They are the special cases of standard form $Ax + By = C$ where $A$ or $B$ is $0$.

On a horizontal line every point has the same height. Through $(2, 3)$, that height is $3$, so every point satisfies $y = 3$, whatever $x$ is. The rise between any two points is $0$, so the slope is $\frac{0}{\text{run}} = 0$. On a vertical line every point has the same $x$: through $(2, 3)$ it is $x = 2$. Now the run is $0$, and $\frac{\text{rise}}{0}$ is not a number: a vertical line has no slope (its slope is undefined). It is also not a function, since one input, $x = 2$, has many outputs.

blocks.name: linesystem
blocks.cap: The vertical line $x = 2$ and the horizontal line $y = 3$ cross at $(2, 3)$. Drag the test point along each line and watch which coordinate stays fixed.

blocks.html: $y = k$ is horizontal with slope $0$. $x = h$ is vertical with no (undefined) slope. Name the coordinate that never changes.

blocks.title: Through two points
blocks.q: Write the equation of the line through $(-4, 1)$ and $(-4, 6)$.
steps: Both points have $x = -4$, so the run is $0$ and the line is vertical.

blocks.title: Perpendicular to a horizontal line
blocks.q: Write the line through $(5, -2)$ perpendicular to $y = 7$.
steps: $y = 7$ is horizontal, so a perpendicular line is vertical.

blocks.html: Graphing $x = 3$ as a horizontal line, and saying a vertical line has slope $0$. The equation $x = 3$ fixes $x$, so the points are $(3, 0)$, $(3, 1)$, $(3, -2)$: they stack vertically. Its run is $0$, so the slope is undefined; slope $0$ belongs to horizontal lines.
